newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Gazprom moves on Black Sea link to Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Russian Gazprom moves on Black Sea link to Turkey.

text.p: Russia's RAO Gazprom said on Thursday that its board of directors had approved a $2.5 billion project to build the world's deepest underwater gas pipeline linking Russia and Turkey via the Black Sea.

But officials said Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas company, would not issue paper to finance the link, and would instead attract credits from joint ventures planned with Turkish state pipeline company Botas for the project.

"We do not connect the issue of the Eurobond to the Turkish link," Yenal Yermolayev, Gazprom's deputy director of strategic developments, told a news conference. "We will use other financing sources."
Gazprom, which raised $429 million from a placement of American Depositary Shares in London last year, plans to issue a Eurobond in 1997.
The 1,055 km (655 mile) link, known as the eastern link, will carry 16 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year to Turkey, with initial supplies of three bcm a year to begin in 2000.
About 380 km (235 miles) of the link will lie in the Black Sea at a depth of 2.1 km (1.3 miles) below sea level.
Gazprom officials said analogous projects existed in the North Sea and Gulf of Mexico but that they were not as far below sea level and had smaller diameter pipelines with less pressure.

"The Black Sea pipeline will be in waters twice as deep as anything else and the pipeline diameter will be twice as thick as anything else," said Harry van der Hayden, general manager of Petergaz, a joint venture between Gazprom and private Dutch offshore contractor Hareema.
He said Petergaz would complete a six-month feasibility study for the project by May or June.

The proposed Black Sea pipeline will run from the Izobilnaya compressor station in southern Russia, 100 km (62 miles) east of Krasnodar, to the Black Sea outlet Dzhugba and across the Black Sea to an as yet unspecified point in eastern Turkey.

Vladimir Poddubsky, a senior Gazprom engineer, said an alternative land-based route through the former Soviet Caucasian republics of Georgia and Armenia was scrapped because it was more circuitous and cost $500 million more than the sea link.
Yermolayev said Russian gas supplies to Turkey now total six bcm via an existing pipeline, known as the western route, that traverses Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria.
Supplies via that route -- whose Turkish portion will hook into the Black Sea link's own proposed Turkish section -- would rise to 14 bcm in the next millenium.
Total Russian gas supplies to Turkey via all routes would reach 30 bcm, Yermolayev said, adding that Romania, Bulgaria, Macedonia, Greece and Albania would still receive supplies.
